The equivalent MV SST model for power flow was implemented and tested in OpenDSS and the reactive power functionality was developed. Five different sites were chosen as the high-power EV charging sites. The use case scenarios were developed to study the value of SST on the distribution feeder in presence of high EV charging. Using SST instead of conventional transformers showed the improved voltage profile, reduced substation reactive power demand, maintained the secondary side voltage at 1 per unit, and regulated the MV side voltage. Therefore, SST can benefit local sites by regulating voltage. It was observed that the regulators and capacitors installed at different locations in the feeder help maintain the overall feeder voltage, while having SST can benefit with improved voltages at conditions where regulators and capacitors were not able to maintain the voltage. The 31 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications. result analysis suggests that the integration of MV SSTs into the grid has the potential to enhance EV charging infrastructure, DER operation, and grid performance significantly. As the number of MV SSTs is increased, it is reasonable to expect even more substantial benefits for the overall grid stability and efficiency. This research paves the way for further exploration and deployment of MV SSTs in power distribution systems to accommodate the increasing demand for EV charging while ensuring optimal grid operation. Furthermore, the economic analysis indicates that an MV DCFC-configured SST could much more economically serve DCFC loads than T-R- D configurations. This represents a potential opportunity for electric utilities to provide DCFC service more cost-effectively through economic application of MV DCFC-configured SSTs. Additionally, further investigation into the coordinated operation of MV SSTs and the existing voltage regulators on the grid can be beneficial for the optimal operation of both devices.
